transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-23
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 49 minutes
Attendees: Liam Park (Redwood AE), Sofia Martinez (Redwood SE), Grace Chen (Redwood CSM), Rajiv Kapoor (Apex Head of ML), Maya Thompson (Platform), Oliver Grant (Security), Priya Desai (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): walked through Redwood Console JSON mode, demoed a safe-invoke flow with typed output, discussed guardrail patterns (schema enforcement, fallback to text, canary rollouts), reviewed pilot success criteria and security requirements.

Transcript:
[00:00] Liam: alright everyone thanks for joining, uh this is Liam from Redwood, i'm joined by Sofia who will do the deep dive. quick agenda: console walkthrough, api and runtime patterns for safe invoke, then pilot scoping.
[00:18] Rajiv: hey thanks, quick thing — our team needs deterministic JSON to feed into our order funnel, we can't have random free text. latency target is < 100ms p50 for short prompts — is that realistic?
[00:34] Sofia: yeah great question. so two levers there — model selection + runtime optimizations. in JSON mode we enforce schema up front so the model outputs a typed payload, and the runtime has a fallback if the schema fails. note: sometimes the transcription says schema validation fails and we fall back to an extractor step which tries to patch the output.
[00:52] Oliver: when you say fallback can you give example? if the model doesn't emit valid JSON, do you retry? do you hit another model?
[00:59] Sofia: good — we have a configurable fallback chain. default is: 1) quick re-prompt with a tighter instruction, 2) if still invalid, route to a lighter-weight deterministic extractor service (like a regex-based parser) or 3) call an alternative model variant pinned for safety. you'd define the policy in the Console. sometimes we call it safe-invoke.
[01:21] Maya: what about tool calling — we plan to call an inventory service and a pricing microservice. how do you protect that?
[01:28] Sofia: we demoed tool contracts — you declare the function signature with a JSON schema and Redwood validates the arguments before invoking the service. there's also a dry-run sandbox where the runtime will simulate the call and show the payload in the Console. again, think of it like typechecking for runtime calls.
[01:46] Rajiv: is there network isolation for those calls? we need them to run inside our VPC and not leave the private network.
[01:53] Grace: yes — for Private or Dedicated we support VPC peering and private egress for tool invocation, plus KMS integration for secrets so downstream calls use customer-managed keys.
[02:05] Priya: quick note — our security team will ask for audit trail per-token, is that available?
[02:11] Liam: yep, per-request tracing and audit logs with token-level metadata. we can provide log retention options and an exported event stream if needed.
[02:20] Sofia: i'll jump to the Console demo — i'm sharing my screen. sorry if the demo quality is a bit rough; recording will be shared.
[02:30] [screen share noises] Sofia: ok here is the project view, we have an example "order-normalizer" schema. see the required fields: order_id string, items array of objects with sku, qty, price, and a normalized_total. i'll trigger the JSON mode endpoint with a sample prompt.
[02:51] Sofia: hit run — runtime returns a typed JSON blob, highlighted in green. note the validator caught a missing price and the fallback applied a patch: it filled price from our product catalog lookup (in the simulated sandbox) and flagged the correction. transcription sometimes shows that as "KV cash lookup" — it's KV cache, sorry.
[03:11] Oliver: the correction flag — can you surface that to downstream? we need a boolean to mark patched outputs so consumers can decide to re-ingest.
[03:18] Sofia: yes there's a metadata field in the response: validation_status with values like valid|patched|failed and a corrections array. you can route patched results to a separate queue.
[03:29] Rajiv: great. what about performance implications of the validator and patcher? does it add a lot of latency?
[03:34] Sofia: small overhead, typically single-digit ms for simple schemas. the bigger cost is model re-invokes. to mitigate we recommend prefix caching and batching when appropriate; Redwood Optimize will suggest batching windows based on your token distribution.
[03:49] Maya: can you pin models? we need stable behaviour across releases.
[03:52] Liam: yes you can pin model versions in the deployment config and use rollouts — canary or A/B. if a new version introduces schema regressions, we have automatic regression alerts tied to prompt test sets.
[04:06] Priya: on encryption — is request and KV cache encrypted with our KMS?
[04:11] Grace: yes, in Private/Dedicated we integrate with customer KMS for encrypting persistent caches and logs. ephemeral memory is in-process but we provide controls.
[04:20] Sofia: moving back to tool safety — demoing the function contract editor now. you define name, inputs (JSON schema) and a set of allowed HTTP endpoints. the runtime will validate and then sign the request with a short-lived token. in the sandbox it shows the signed payload.
[04:42] Rajiv: for our inventory API we need an idempotency token and rate limits — can the function contract declare headers and required metadata?
[04:49] Sofia: yep, you can declare required headers and Redwood will reject attempts to call without them. rate limiting and per-service throughput guards are configured on the gateway side; we can integrate into your API gateway via VPC private endpoints.
[05:03] Liam: we're hearing that Apex cares about predictable latency, strong schema enforcement, and secure VPC-bound tooling. does that sound right?
[05:09] Rajiv: yep and also deterministic outputs so downstream ETL doesn't break.
[05:13] Priya: one other ask — we'd like the Console to export a set of example payloads for QA. can you provide that?
[05:18] Sofia: absolutely — the sandbox can export generated payloads and you can download a CSV/NDJSON for QA runs.
[05:25] [Demo continued with a small failure case]
[05:30] Sofia: here's an example where the model returned a stray comment line and invalid JSON. the runtime's quick re-prompt fixed it on attempt 2, but our instrumentation shows the second call is slightly higher latency. you can tune the fallback policy threshold so you only retry once.
[05:50] Oliver: in an extreme case we may want to block auto-invokes and send for human review — is that supported?
[05:55] Sophia: (laughter) yeah — we have an "approval gate" policy where any patched or failed output for certain routes goes to a manual review queue.
[06:05] Rajiv: if we do a pilot, what does success look like?
[06:08] Liam: mutually defined: 1) schema pass rate > 98% on our production test set, 2) p50 latency <100ms for the normal short path, 3) integration with Apex VPC and KMS and visible audit logs.
[06:21] Priya: timeline — we'd like a 6-week pilot starting mid-december.
[06:25] Liam: ok we can do that — i'll send an SOW that outlines the dedicated pool size, SLAs, and milestone plan.
[06:31] [customer questions dive deeper]
[06:34] Maya: technical — how do you handle KV cache for personalized prefixes? we can't have cross-tenant leakage.
[06:40] Sofia: per-tenant KV spaces, encrypted at rest and scoped to customer keys. on Dedicated we can also pin GPUs to tenant pools for extra isolation. sometimes the transcript says "pin to VGPUs" — we mean GPU isolation.
[06:55] Rajiv: curious about cost — what's rough per-million token for dedicated vs hosted?
[06:59] Liam: i'll put exact numbers in the SOW but expect lower unit cost on Dedicated with reserved capacity. Redwood Optimize will recommend quantization levels and batching to reduce cost further.
[07:10] Oliver: SOC2 + ISO docs — can you share?
[07:13] Grace: yes we'll share SOC2 type II report and a compliance pack; they're in the security folder we'll send.
[07:20] [recap and next steps]
[07:22] Liam: recap: we'll send SOW and pricing (Liam), Sofia will share the console recording and schemas (Sofia), Apex to provide sample traffic and VPC diagram (Maya/Rajiv). Pilot target mid-december.
[07:36] Rajiv: sounds good, appreciated the demo.
[07:39] Priya: thanks everyone.
[07:41] Liam: thanks all, we'll follow up via email.

End of transcript.

Notes about transcription quality: occasional mis-heard words for "KV cache" -> "KV cash"; speaker label noise around cross-talk at 05:55.
